215: I have just had a sad adventure, which will drive me away from here.
I lose all patience! Death! There is no remedy for it; and you alone are to blame, for you urged and pushed me into a post I was by no means suited to.
I have reason to be satisfied now, and so have you!
But so that you may not again put this disaster down to my impetuous temper, I send you, my dear sir, a plain and simple account of the affair, such as a mere chronicler of facts would give.
216: The Count of O— likes me and singles me out.
That is well known, and I have told you so a hundred times.
Yesterday I dined with him.
It is the day on which the nobility are accustomed to gather at his house in the evening.
I never once thought of the assembly, nor that we subalterns do not belong in such company.
Well, I dined with the count; and after dinner we went through to the large hall.
We walked up and down together, and I talked with him, and with Colonel B—, who joined us; and so the hour of the assembly came on.

God knows I was thinking of nothing, when in came the honourable Lady with her noble husband and their silly, scheming daughter, with her small waist and flat neck; and with disdainful looks and a haughty air they passed me by.

As I heartily detest the whole breed, I decided to go; and I was only waiting for the count to free himself from their impertinent prattle so that I could take my leave, when the agreeable Miss B— came in.

As I never meet her without a heartfelt pleasure, I stayed and talked to her, leaning over the back of her chair, and it was some time before I noticed that she seemed a little confused, and had stopped answering me with her usual ease.
It struck me.
"Heavens!" I said to myself. "Can she be like the rest of them too?"
I felt annoyed and was on the point of leaving; but I stayed all the same, making excuses for her, fancying she did not mean it, and still hoping for some friendly sign.
The rest of the company now arrived.

There was Baron F—, in a whole suit dating from the coronation of Francis I; the Chancellor N—, with his deaf wife; and the shabbily dressed I—, whose old-fashioned coat showed evidence of modern repairs, which crowned the whole.
I talked with some of my acquaintances, but they answered me in monosyllables.

I was busy watching Miss B—, and did not notice that the women were whispering at the end of the room, that the murmur was spreading by degrees to the men, and that Madame S— was addressing the count very warmly.
All this was related to me afterwards by Miss B—.
At length the count came up to me and took me over to the window.
"You know our ridiculous customs," he said.
"I see that the company is rather displeased at your being here. I would not on any account —"
"I beg your excellency's pardon!" I exclaimed.
"I ought to have thought of it before, but I know you will forgive this little inattention."
"I was going some time ago," I added, "but my evil genius kept me here."
And I smiled and bowed, and took my leave.
He shook me by the hand in a way that said everything.
I hurried straight out of the illustrious assembly, sprang into a carriage, and drove to M—.
I watched the sun set from the top of the hill, and read that beautiful passage in Homer where Ulysses is entertained by the hospitable herdsmen.
That was delightful indeed.
217: I came home to supper in the evening.
There were only a few people in the room.
They had turned back a corner of the tablecloth and were playing dice.
He laid down his hat when he saw me, came over, and said in a low voice, "You have met with a disagreeable adventure."
"The count obliged you to leave the assembly!"
"I was very glad to be out of it."
"I am delighted," he added, "that you take it so lightly."
"I am only sorry that it is already so much talked about."
It was then that the thing began to hurt.
I fancied that everyone who sat down, or even looked at me, was thinking of this incident; and my heart grew bitter.
218: And now I could plunge a dagger into my breast, when I hear myself pitied on every side, and see the triumph of my enemies.
This is always the way with vain people, they say — people whose heads are turned with conceit, who make a show of despising forms and such petty, idle nonsense.
219: Say what you like about fortitude, but show me the man who can patiently endure the laughter of fools when they have got the advantage of him.
It is only when their nonsense has no foundation that one can bear it without complaint.
221: I met Miss B— out walking today.
I could not help joining her; and when we were a little way from her companions, I told her I had felt the change in her manner toward me.
"O Werther!" she said, in a tone of emotion, "you, who know my heart, how could you so misread my distress?"
"What did I not suffer for you, from the moment you came into that room!"
"I foresaw it all; a hundred times I was on the point of telling you."
"I knew that the S——s and T——s, with their husbands, would leave the room rather than stay in your company."
"I knew the count would not break with them — and now there is so much talk about it."
"How!" I exclaimed, and tried to hide my emotion; for everything Adelin had told me the day before came back painfully at that moment.
"Oh, how much it has already cost me!" said this amiable girl, while her eyes filled with tears.
I could scarcely contain myself, and was ready to throw myself at her feet.
She wiped them away without trying to hide them.
"You know my aunt," she went on. "She was there — and in what light do you suppose she sees the affair!"
"Last night, and again this morning, Werther, I had to sit through a lecture on my acquaintance with you."
"I have had to hear you condemned and belittled, and I could not — I dared not — say much in your defence."
222: Every word she said was a dagger in my heart.
She did not feel what a mercy it would have been to keep all of it from me.
She told me besides all the impertinence that would go on circulating, and how the malicious would gloat.
How they would rejoice at the punishment of my pride, at my humiliation for that want of regard for others I have so often been reproached with.
To hear all this, Wilhelm, spoken by her in a voice of the most sincere sympathy, roused every passion in me; and I am still in a state of extreme agitation.
I wish I could find a man to jeer at me about this business.
I would sacrifice him to my resentment.
The sight of his blood might possibly relieve my fury.
A hundred times I have taken up a dagger to give this oppressed heart some ease.
Naturalists tell of a noble breed of horses that instinctively open a vein with their teeth when they are heated and exhausted by a long run, in order to breathe more freely.
I am often tempted to open a vein, and secure myself everlasting liberty.
224: I have tendered my resignation to the court.
I hope it will be accepted, and you will forgive me for not having consulted you first.
It is necessary that I leave this place.
I know everything you will say to make me stay, and so I beg you will soften the news to my mother.
I am unable to do anything for myself; how then should I be fit to help others?
It will grieve her that I should have broken off the career that would have made me first a privy councillor and then a minister, and that I should be looking backwards instead of advancing.
Argue as you like, gather up every reason that should have kept me here — I am going, and that is enough.
But so that you may know where I am bound, I may mention that the Prince of —— is here.
He is much pleased with my company; and having heard of my intention to resign, he has invited me to his country house to spend the spring months with him.
I shall be left completely my own master; and as we agree on everything but one point, I shall try my fortune and go with him.
226: Thank you for both your letters.
I delayed my reply, and held this letter back, until I should have an answer from the court.
I feared my mother might apply to the minister to thwart my purpose.
But my request is granted; my resignation is accepted.
I shall not recount how reluctantly it was granted, nor what the minister has written: you would only start your lamentations again.
The crown prince has sent me a present of twenty-five ducats, and such goodness has moved me to tears.
For that reason I shall not need the money from my mother that I asked for lately.
228: I leave this place tomorrow; and since my native town is only six miles off the high road, I mean to visit it once more and call back the happy dreams of my childhood.
I shall go in at the same gate I came out of with my mother, when, after my father's death, she left that delightful retreat to shut herself up in your melancholy town.
Adieu, my dear friend; you shall hear how I get on.
230: I have paid my visit to my native town with all the devotion of a pilgrim, and have felt many emotions I did not expect.

Near the great elm, a quarter of a league from the village, I got out of the carriage and sent it on ahead, so that alone and on foot I might enjoy all the pleasure of my recollections vividly and with my whole heart.
I stood there under the same elm that was once the goal and end of all my walks.
Then, in happy ignorance, I longed for a world I did not know, where I hoped to find every pleasure and enjoyment my heart could want.
And now, coming back from that wide world, O my friend, how many disappointed hopes and failed plans I have brought back with me!
231: As I looked at the mountains stretched out before me, I thought how often they had been the object of my dearest wishes.
Here I used to sit for hours with my eyes fixed on them, longing to wander in the shade of those woods and lose myself in those valleys that look so delightful from a distance.
How unwillingly I used to leave this charming spot when my hour of recreation was over and my leave had expired!
I came near the village and knew all the old summerhouses and gardens again; I disliked the new ones, and every other alteration that had been made.
I went into the village, and all my former feelings came back.
I cannot go into details, my dear friend, charming as my sensations were: they would be dull in the telling.
I had meant to lodge in the market-place, near our old house.
As soon as I went in, I saw that the schoolroom where that good old woman taught us as children had been turned into a shop.
I remembered the sorrow, the heaviness, the tears, the oppression of heart I felt in that confinement.
Every step brought its own particular impression.
A pilgrim in the Holy Land does not meet so many places charged with tender recollections, nor is his soul moved with much greater devotion.
One incident will serve as an illustration.
I followed the course of a stream down to a farm — once a favourite walk of mine — and stopped at the spot where, as boys, we used to amuse ourselves skimming stones across the water.
I remembered so clearly how I used to watch the course of that same stream, following it with eager curiosity, forming romantic ideas about the countries it would pass through.
But my imagination was soon exhausted, while the water went on flowing further and further, until my fancy was lost in the thought of an invisible distance.
Exactly so, my dear friend, so happy and so confined, were the thoughts of our good ancestors.
Their feelings and their poetry were as fresh as childhood.
And when Ulysses speaks of the immeasurable sea and the boundless earth, his words are true, natural, deeply felt, and full of mystery.
What does it matter that I have learned, along with every schoolboy, that the world is round?
A man needs little earth to enjoy himself on, and less still for his final rest.
232: I am at present with the prince at his hunting lodge.
He is a man one can live happily with.
There are, however, some strange characters about him whom I cannot make out at all.
They do not seem vicious, and yet they do not look thoroughly honest either.
Sometimes I am inclined to think them honest, and still I cannot bring myself to trust them.
It grieves me to hear the prince talk now and then of things he has only read or heard about, and always from the point of view in which others have presented them.
233: He values my understanding and my talents more highly than my heart, and my heart is the only thing I am proud of.
It is the sole source of everything — of our strength, our happiness, and our misery.
All the knowledge I have, anyone else can acquire; but my heart is mine alone.
235: I have had a plan in my head which I did not mean to speak of until it was accomplished; now that it has failed, I may as well tell you.
I wanted to enter the army, and had wished to take that step for a long time.
It was indeed the chief reason for my coming here with the prince, since he is a general in the service.
I told him my design during one of our walks together.
He disapproved of it, and it would have been sheer madness not to listen to his reasons.
237: Say what you like, I can stay here no longer.
Time hangs heavy on my hands.
The prince is as gracious to me as anyone could be, and yet I am not at my ease.
There is nothing in common between us.
He is a man of understanding, but quite of the ordinary kind.
His conversation gives me no more amusement than I should get from reading a well-written book.
I shall stay a week longer, and then set out on my travels again.
My drawings are the best things I have done since I came here.
The prince has a taste for the arts, and would improve if his mind were not fettered by cold rules and mere technical notions.

I often lose patience when, with a glowing imagination, I am giving expression to art and nature, and he breaks in with learned suggestions and throws about the technical phrases of artists at random.
239: Once more I am a wanderer, a pilgrim through the world.
241: I will tell you in confidence.
I am obliged to stay here another fortnight, and then I think it would be better for me to visit the mines in ——.
But I am only deceiving myself with that.
The fact is, I want to be near Charlotte again; that is all.
I smile at what my heart suggests, and I obey it.
243: No, no! It is well yet — all is well!
O God, who gave me being, if you had destined this happiness for me, my whole life would have been one long thanksgiving.
But I will not complain — forgive these tears, forgive these fruitless wishes.
Oh, the very thought of folding the dearest of Heaven's creatures in my arms!
Dear Wilhelm, my whole frame is convulsed when I see Albert put his arm around her slender waist.
244: She would have been happier with me than with him.
Albert is not the man to satisfy the wishes of such a heart.
He lacks a certain sensibility; he lacks — in short, their hearts do not beat together.
How often, my dear friend, reading a passage in some interesting book, have my heart and Charlotte's seemed to meet!
And in a hundred other moments, when our feelings were drawn out by the story of some imaginary character, I have felt that we were made for one another.
But, dear Wilhelm, he loves her with his whole soul; and what does a love like that not deserve?
245: I have been interrupted by an insufferable visit.
I have dried my tears and composed my thoughts.
